Lists on-readings ブン・モン and kun-readings きく・きこえる. Senses include hear/be audible, learn by hearing, rumor/reputation, and smell (聞香).
evidence.title: 聞 | 漢字一字 | 漢字ペディア

evidence.text: 聞く means to hear sounds or speech, accept/heed, ask, and smell or assess aroma/flavor; it gives examples including 鳥のさえずりを聞く, 忠告を聞く, 道を聞く, and 茶の香りを聞く.
evidence.title: き－く | 言葉 | 漢字ペディア

evidence.text: 〈聞道〉・〈聞説〉 is read きくならく and means ‘I hear that…’ or ‘according to what I hear’. This is a literary expression; it can illustrate a kun reading only in this lexicalized phrase, not as ordinary spelling of 聞く.
evidence.title: きくならく | 言葉 | 漢字ペディア

evidence.text: Reports the oracle-bone form as a person cupping the mouth with a hand and raising the ear to listen (attributed to 于省吾); another account interprets the hand/ear dots as sound entering the ear (張世超等). It cites oracle-bone examples for hearing/knowing (合集2422) and for ‘news’ (合集6077). These are scholarly interpretations of the depicted form, not settled descriptions of an object.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 | 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.text: Says that in bronze forms the ear separates from the human figure; two dots develop into shapes resembling 小 or 尔, and a 止-like form below the person is later corrupted to 女. It describes Warring States phonetic forms with 耳+昏 (matching 說文古文 䎽) and 耳+門 (Qin-system form continued in the current graph). 說文 states 聞 ‘知聞也。从耳，門聲’ and 䎽 ‘古文从昏’.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 | 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.text: Cites bronze inscription ‘我聞殷述令’ on the Great Yu ding for hearing/receiving a command, and bronze inscriptions for sound or reputation spreading widely. It separately records borrowed uses of 聞 for 問, 昏, and 婚; those are graph borrowings, not evidence that these are graphic components. It cites later textual senses: news/experience in Analects 季氏, being heard of or famous in Guodian 語叢四 and 史記 五帝本紀, transmission in 詩經 小雅 鶴鳴, and smelling in 韓非子 十過 and 論衡 四諱. The database provides work/inscription identifiers but not absolute dates for every cited witness.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 | 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: 楊明明, Fudan University Center for Research on Unearthed Texts and Ancient Chinese Writing
evidence.text: Describes oracle-bone 聞 as a person with a hand at the mouth and an ear, while reporting that 董作賓 interpreted it as a person kneeling and covering the mouth to report. It notes early Western Zhou bronze forms close to oracle-bone forms, later graphic corruption, and 說文’s contrast between ancient 耳+昏 and seal 耳+門. It cites 大盂鼎 inscription 02837 ‘我聞殷述令’ for the hearing sense and separate bronze uses borrowed for 婚 and another graph. This is a real interpretive difference about the oracle form’s action/context; it does not establish that the modern 門-shaped portion came from an ancient 門.
evidence.title: 楊明明：釋毛公鼎“庸有聞”及相關問題

evidence.text: The database distinguishes direct early hearing/knowing examples from later or separate usages: news/knowledge, reputation, propagation, smell, and bronze inscription loans for 問, 昏, and 婚. The listed examples establish attested uses, but do not by themselves prove every semantic transition or its precise chronology.

It gives a 1001–1014 源氏物語 example for asking, and a 1275 名語記 example for smelling incense. These Japanese word attestations document Japanese senses independently of the Chinese graph’s history.

evidence.field: Early graph interpretations and graphic development
evidence.text: The database reports an oracle-bone interpretation, attributed to 于省吾, of a person covering the mouth with a hand and raising the ear to listen. It also reports an alternative account that dots by the hand or ear represent sound entering the ear. Bronze forms separate the ear from the human figure; dots develop into forms resembling 小 or 尔; and a 止-like shape below the person is later corrupted to 女. The database identifies Warring States forms with 耳+昏, matching the Shuowen ancient form, and a Qin-system 耳+門 form continuing in the current graph. These are reported interpretations of the forms, not a settled account of every oracle-bone detail.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 | 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.field: Early senses, later uses, and graph loans
evidence.text: Cites oracle-bone examples for hearing/knowing (合集2422) and ‘news’ (合集6077), without giving absolute dates for those individual inscriptions. It cites the Great Yu ding’s ‘我聞殷述令’ for hearing or receiving a command, and other bronze examples for sound or reputation spreading widely. It separately records graph loans for 問, 昏, and 婚, which are whole-graph borrowed uses rather than components of the form. It cites later transmitted or excavated texts for news/experience, fame, dissemination, and smell. The attestations establish distinct uses; the source does not by itself establish a continuous semantic chronology among them.

It notes early Western Zhou bronze forms close to oracle-bone forms and cites the Great Yu ding inscription 02837, ‘我聞殷述令,’ for the hearing sense. etymology_notes.text: Phonosemantic compound. 耳 represents the meaning and 門 represents the sound.

etymology_notes.caveat: Classical source (~100 AD). Some etymologies may be incorrect by modern scholarship.

etymology_notes.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *mɯn, *mɯns): phonetic 門 (OC *mɯːn) + semantic 耳 (“ear”). Compare 問 (OC *mɯns).
Schuessler derives this from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *mnəm (“to smell”), whence Tibetan མནམ་པ (mnam pa, “to smell of”), Tibetan སྣོམ་པ (snom pa, “to smell”), Jingpho manam (mə³¹ nam⁵⁵, “smell”), Burmese နမ် (nam, “to smell”), Burmese နံ (nam, “to stink”) (Schuessler, 2007). It is very phonetically difficult, requiring an inversion of n and m in Chinese (which Schuessler attributes to labial dissimilation or prefix-preemption) in addition to rejecting the Baxter-Sagart reconstruction with a *u in favour of reconstructing *ə instead (*u and *ə are difficult to distinguish before *-n). The reconstruction with *u is solidified by rhyming patterns in the Classic of Poetry, making Schuessler's etymology impossible.
In almost all major Tibeto-Burman languages, this etymon means only "to smell". Schuessler explains the application of "to hear" in Chinese via various influences. He sees a parallel in Tibeto-Burman *na "ear ~ nose" and hence perhaps in Sino-Tibetan (see *r/g-na (“ear”)). The Chinese stem may have converged with a Mon-Khmer etymon (cf. Proto-Monic *smaaɲ (“to inquire”) (ibid.). Schuessler also notes Tibetan མཉན་པ (mnyan pa, “to listen to; to hear”), which he deems phonologically quite close to Chinese.
Pronunciation 2 ("be heard about; renowned; fame") is a derivation of pronunciation 1, with passive suffix *-s (ibid.).
問 (OC *mɯns, “to ask”) is the exoactive derivation of pronunciation 1 with suffix *-s, literally "let (me) hear" (ibid.).

duan_notes.note: 往曰聽。來曰聞。大學曰。心不在焉。聽而不聞。引申之爲令聞廣譽。

shuowen.english: know, perceive, comprehend and hear. Composed of 耳 (semantic) and 門 (phonetic).

context.japanese_editorial_instructions:
Write an English-language etymology entry for a JAPANESE learner, about the
Japanese graph named in this dossier. The historical graph may originate in China, but current
Japanese readings and senses are separate research questions. The source_reuse packet is a
reviewed prior Chinese research starting point, not an approved Japanese article. Consult local
sources AND external Japanese dictionary references; verify citations before transferring claims.
Use authoritative Japanese dictionaries (Kanjipedia, KANJIDIC2/JMdict, scholarly sources) for
Japanese readings and senses, and Cultural Affairs form tables for documented form conventions.
Write independently. Reuse supported historical facts, source records and exact-graph glyphs;
do not transfer modern Chinese usage, meaning history, Mandarin learner sound comparisons or
components from a different graph. Inspect prior_analysis as a lead and correct it where needed.
For shinjitai, distinguish the Japanese current form, kyujitai, and simplified Chinese; similarity
alone is not proof of shared reform history. A counterpart's images remain explicitly scoped to
that counterpart. Do not infer a Japanese-created character merely from its absence in Chinese.
Learner overview starts with useful Japanese meaning and a sourced logical current component
split. Keep ancient Chinese sound roles separate from Japanese on/kun readings. A Chinese
phonetic role need not predict a kun reading. If comparing Japanese on readings, provide supported
component and host readings; matching current readings alone do not prove historical phonetic
formation. Mandarin comparisons belong only in clearly labeled expert historical context when
actually useful, never as the Japanese learner default.
Include language="ja" and japanese_usage: summary plus 2-4 selected reading records (1 if only
one useful reading is supported), with type on/kun/special, reading in kana, an actual example
containing the entry graph, full example_reading in kana, a concise English gloss, and explanation.
Examples and readings require inspected Japanese lexical evidence, not invented combinations.
Check the reading/example association itself: a compound listed on a character page may
illustrate a different reading. For example, an on-reading word cannot illustrate a kun-reading
card. Verify whole-word spelling, full reading, gloss and selected character reading together.
Use unambiguous examples for kun cards; leave altered or irregular readings to separately
supported explanations. Reviewer verification must check these associations explicitly.
Prefer beginner-useful examples; do not claim JLPT membership of an example without evidence.
Kun dictionary dots mark okurigana, not literal spelling. Special readings such as jukujikun
belong to whole words and must not be assigned mechanically to individual components. Explain
multiple readings briefly without dumping all dictionary readings or nanori. Cite usage and
reading claims. On readings are historically borrowed; kun readings associate Japanese words
with the graph, not Chinese pronunciations. State only source-supported transmission details.
Meaning_history distinguishes early graph/Chinese word history from established Japanese uses;
do not invent a continuous semantic path between them. Inspect Japanese attestations where
available and record gaps. Write neutral reader prose; bibliography specifics stay in citations.
Reviewers must evaluate the Japanese adaptation, lexical examples, form scopes, reuse provenance
and all ordinary factual/readability gates independently. An approved Chinese entry is not a
Japanese approval.
